analysis.one_liner: Bans most noncompete agreements that stop workers from taking a new job.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make noncompete agreements unenforceable for ordinary employees, ending the common practice of requiring workers to sign contracts that bar them from joining a competitor or starting a similar business after leaving a job. It preserves narrow exceptions: a seller of a business can agree not to open a competing shop in the area where the business operated, and a top executive leaving as part of a sale can accept a paid, one-year noncompete. Employers would still be able to protect trade secrets and confidential information with nondisclosure agreements. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and received no further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by noncompetes. The bill's own findings cite economists' estimate that 1 in 5 U.S. workers is covered by one, and state that noncompetes reduce wages, restrict mobility, and slow innovation [S3]. Anyone who has signed such an agreement could change jobs freely, negotiate with competing employers, or start a similar business without facing a lawsuit.

how_it_helps.text: Makes new noncompete agreements void and bans employers from entering into, enforcing, or attempting to enforce them against employees and contractors [S3].

Gives workers multiple ways to fight back: complaints to the FTC and Labor Department, a private lawsuit with attorney's fees, and state attorney general actions; it also bars forced arbitration or class-action waivers for these claims [S3].
Requires employers to post workplace notices about the ban and directs the FTC and Labor Department to build shared enforcement standards and confidential complaint systems [S3].

Preserves legitimate employer protections: trade secret and confidentiality agreements remain fully valid, and business sellers and paid senior executives in a sale may still accept narrow, time-limited noncompetes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who rely on noncompetes to hold onto trained staff and keep departing workers from helping competitors. Businesses across sectors would have to compete for labor on wages and conditions rather than contract restrictions, and would bear the cost of workplace notices and potential FTC or Labor Department enforcement [S3].

drawbacks.text: The sale-of-business exception lets owners of at least 5 percent of a company, and highly paid senior executives with severance packages, sign enforceable noncompetes, so the restriction remains available to people at the top [S3].
Employers keep full freedom to use nondisclosure and trade secret agreements, which can function in practice as a quieter way to limit where a former worker can go [S3].
Dual enforcement by both the FTC and the Labor Department, with regulations required within 18 months, creates overlap and compliance costs that businesses would bear [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the estimated one in five workers bound by noncompetes, the benefit is direct: higher bargaining power and the freedom to change jobs. Employers lose a tool for retaining staff, which could raise their recruiting and training costs, but the bill preserves the narrower legal tools (trade secrets, NDAs) that protect genuine business interests. The main design question is the carve-outs for business sellers and senior executives, which preserve noncompetes for the best-paid while eliminating them for everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on February 1, 2023 with three cosponsors across both parties: Republicans Todd Young and Kevin Cramer and Democrat Tim Kaine [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
That referral was the bill's last recorded action; no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote appears in the action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use noncompete agreements keep their existing ability to restrict departing workers. No state or federal ban was preempted, and the status quo of largely state-regulated noncompetes continues.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were bipartisan (two Democrats, two Republicans), but the bill never advanced far enough for a party-line vote to occur.

industries.industry: Employers across sectors that use noncompetes
industries.note: The bill would void noncompetes against rank-and-file workers, forcing employers to retain staff through pay and conditions rather than contract restrictions. Because it never advanced, these employers retain the status quo.

industries.industry: Trade secret and employment law practice (law firms, compliance)
industries.note: A federal ban would have reshaped employment contracts and generated enforcement work for FTC and Labor Department proceedings and private suits. The bill's failure leaves existing state-by-state law and the employer-favorable contracting market in place.
